title: Former feds sue Office of Special Counsel over its response to mass probationary firings
summary: Former federal employees are suing the Office of Special Counsel over its response to the mass probationary firings earlier this year., after OSC ended its investigation into thousands of complaints that probationary employees had sent to the agency.
content:
By Drew Friedman

Former federal employees are suing the Office of Special Counsel over the agency’s response to the mass probationary firings that took place earlier this year.

The legal action comes after OSC ended its investigation into thousands of complaints that probationary employees had sent to the agency — and reversed its previous opinion to say it now believed agencies had not been firing enough probationary workers. Attorneys from Democracy Forward are representing the former employees in the case and filed the lawsuit Wednesday.

“By closing the door on thousands of dedicated public servants who were unlawfully laid off, the Trump-Vance administration has transformed the independent Office of Special Counsel into yet another political arm of the White House,” Skye Perryman, president and CEO of Democracy Forward, said in a press statement.

Earlier this year, OSC began investigating more than 2,000 complaints that terminated probationary employees filed with the independent investigative agency, led by then-Special Counsel Hampton Dellinger. At the time, Dellinger said he believed agencies’ firings of probationary employees violated the law.

President Donald Trump fired Dellinger, and when current Acting Special Counsel Jamieson Greer stepped in to lead the investigative agency, OSC subsequently ceased its work looking into the mass firings.

Trump orders more agencies to nix collective bargaining agreements

The plaintiffs in the lawsuit called OSC’s decision to end its investigations of complaints from probationary employees a “categorical exclusion.” Their lawsuit alleges that OSC’s actions violated the Administrative Procedure Act. The plaintiffs are also arguing that the agency’s actions this year ignored OSC’s statutory obligations under Title 5.

A spokesperson for OSC told Federal News Network that the agency does not have a comment on the lawsuit at this time.

The plaintiffs previously worked at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, General Services Administration, Department of Health and Human Services, Environmental Protection Agency and Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

The lawsuit comes after a federal appeals court on Monday ordered the dismissal of a case led by a group of states challenging the Trump administration’s probationary firings.

OSC’s reversed opinion

Following OSC’s leadership turnover this year, the investigative agency also said it believed agencies can fire probationary employees for virtually any reason and at any time.

In May, an amicus brief that OSC sent to the Merit Systems Protection Board reversed its previous legal position and instead argued that current federal regulations give agencies broad discretion to terminate probationers “with very limited restrictions on the reasons for termination.”

OSC also said in May that it believed agencies’ probationary terminations were in compliance with statutory and regulatory requirements and therefore did not constitute prohibited personnel practices. In response to OSC’s amicus brief, attorneys representing employees in their cases before the MSPB called OSC’s actions “unwelcome,” and said the agency overstepped its authority by issuing the brief.

The plaintiffs in the new lawsuit called the agency’s reversed opinion on the probationary firings “unlawful” and “ill-explained.”

“That policy lacks any statutory basis, is an abdication of OSC’s legal mandate, and violates the Administrative Procedure Act (APA),” the lawsuit states.
author: Federal News Network
